narrative:
The model predicted a 69% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5 was the third most important factor; because it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students, it worked in your favor and pulled the prediction somewhat toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your class standings.

Your LSAT score of 27.5 (versus an accepted-student average of 37.2) and low family income also contributed to the negative outlook, though less strongly. Gender and race played no role in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and test scores in a future application would likely change the prediction in your favor.
